## Overview

This [[adyen]] documentation snapshot explains why 3D Secure is used in response to online-payment authentication regulation, surveys region-specific examples and dated scheme changes, and summarizes scheme- and flow-dependent fraud-chargeback liability-shift rules. It complements the integration routes in [[adyen-3d-secure]]; it is not universal legal advice or proof that a particular transaction is compliant, authenticated, authorized, or protected from chargeback liability.

## Key takeaways

- Adyen says many of the surveyed regulations apply to issuing banks rather than directly to merchants, while warning that an issuer may refuse a transaction it evaluates as non-compliant and thereby lower authorization rates. The page routes merchants to regulatory, scheme, EMVCo, and Adyen guidance rather than making its overview a substitute for those authorities.
- The regional section gives examples for Australia, Europe, India, Malaysia, Japan, and France. Applicability varies by actor, geography, transaction type, thresholds, exemptions, and issuer behavior; the dates and card-scheme changes on this collected page are snapshot evidence, not confirmation of current requirements.
- Adyen describes 3D Secure as an extra verification layer for card-not-present transactions. In the native 3DS2 route described here, the issuer authenticates within the merchant website or app using passive, biometric, or two-factor approaches.
- The page states a general fraud-liability rule for a successfully completed 3DS2 challenge and notes that some regions may also grant liability shift after a successful frictionless flow. Its Visa, Mastercard, and Cartes Bancaires rules remain conditioned by scheme, region, period, transaction type, authentication preference, issuer behavior, and flow outcome.

> [!warning] Liability shift is conditional
> Do not infer liability shift merely from 3DS implementation or an apparent success indicator. The page records a rare US domestic Visa case in which issuer CAVV validation can fail and prevent liability shift even when ECI 05 is returned; other scheme-specific exceptions and conditions remain in the raw tables.

quotes.text: Most regulations apply to issuing banks and not to you as a merchant, however, you will get the risk of getting lower authorisation rates if an issuing bank evaluates a transaction as non-compliant, and refuses the transaction as a result.
quotes.location: ## What you need to know (raw line 23)

quotes.text: Here are examples of existing regulations that may apply either to you or to issuing banks if you are conducting business in the following regions:

3D Secure is an authentication protocol that provides an additional layer of verification for card-not-present (CNP) transactions. The protocol is compliant with authentication regulations, including the SCA mandate from PSD2.

The general rule is if a shopper successfully completes a 3D Secure 2 [challenge authentication flow](/online-payments/3d-secure#challenge-flow), the liability for fraudulent chargebacks shifts from you to the card issuer. In a challenge flow, the issuer requires additional shopper interaction. In some regions, card schemes may grant liability shift after a successful [frictionless flow](/online-payments/3d-secure#frictionless-flow), where the transaction is approved after a passive authentication.
quotes.location: ## 3D Secure chargeback liability shift rules (raw line 85)

quotes.text: For US domestic Visa transactions, there are rare cases when the issuer might fail to validate the Cardholder Authentication Verification Value (CAVV) meaning that the transaction does not qualify for a liability shift even though the Electronic Commerce Indicator (ECI) **05** (3DS authentication was successful) value was provided.

## Regulation and liability boundaries

Adyen's regulation-compliance overview is region-, actor-, scheme-, period-, transaction-, issuer-, and flow-dependent. It says many surveyed regulations apply to issuers rather than directly to merchants, although issuer evaluation of non-compliance can reduce authorization rates. The page states a general fraud-liability shift after a successfully completed 3DS2 challenge and says some regions may also grant it after a successful frictionless flow, but its scheme tables contain material exceptions; for example, a rare US domestic Visa CAVV-validation failure can prevent liability shift even when ECI 05 is returned. Treat the regional rules and dated changes as snapshot guidance rather than universal current legal requirements or a guarantee for a transaction.
